questions.q: Name the six Warsaw Pact countries where communist regimes collapsed in 1989, and identify which one experienced a violent overthrow of its leader.
questions.a: Poland, Hungary, East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria, Romania. Romania is the only country where the communist leader (Nicolae Ceaușescu) was violently overthrown and executed (December 25, 1989). A wrong answer — e.g., including Yugoslavia or Albania, or missing East Germany — reveals confusion between the 1989 revolutions and the later Yugoslav wars (node 008) or the Albanian transition (1991-92), indicating the student cannot distinguish the coordinated Eastern Bloc collapse from separate regional trajectories.

questions.q: Explain the difference between the Brezhnev Doctrine (1968) and the Sinatra Doctrine (1988), and why the latter made the 1989 revolutions possible.
questions.a: Brezhnev Doctrine: "limited sovereignty" — USSR claimed right to intervene militarily to preserve socialism in satellite states (used in Czechoslovakia 1968). Sinatra Doctrine (Gorbachev, 1988 UN speech): "they do it their way" — USSR renounced intervention, accepting each country's right to choose its own path. The Sinatra Doctrine removed the existential deterrent: Eastern European reformers knew Soviet tanks would not come, so they could push for change without fear of invasion. A wrong answer that conflates the two doctrines or claims Gorbachev "supported" the revolutions reveals misunderstanding: Gorbachev did not actively support regime change; he merely refused to block it — a crucial distinction for board answers on Soviet agency.

questions.q: In June 1989, Poland held semi-free elections where Solidarity won 160 of 161 contested Sejm seats. In November, East Germans breached the Berlin Wall after Hungary opened its Austrian border in September. Analyze how Poland's negotiated transition and Hungary's border opening created a "demonstration effect" that accelerated the East German collapse.
questions.a: Poland's round-table talks (Feb-Apr 1989) produced a negotiated power-sharing deal: communists kept presidency, Solidarity won contested seats — proving peaceful transition was possible. Hungary's reformist government (May 1989) dismantled the Iron Curtain border fence with Austria (Sept 1989), creating an escape route: 30,000+ East Germans fled via Hungary → Czechoslovakia → West German embassies. This exodus delegitimized the East German regime, triggered mass protests (Leipzig, Oct), and forced the November 9 border opening. The demonstration effect: each success lowered the perceived risk for the next country's protesters. A wrong answer treating these as isolated events misses the transnational diffusion mechanism central to 1989 scholarship.

questions.q: Compare the Czechoslovak "Velvet Revolution" (Nov 17-Dec 29, 1989) and the Romanian Revolution (Dec 16-25, 1989) on three dimensions: (a) role of civil society vs. state security apparatus, (b) level of violence, (c) post-revolution power transfer.
questions.a: (a) Czechoslovakia: Civic Forum (Havel) and Public Against Violence (Slovakia) — broad civil society coalition — negotiated with Communist Party; Romania: spontaneous protests in Timișoara co-opted by National Salvation Front (NSF) — former Party/ Securitate insiders (Iliescu). (b) Czechoslovakia: almost zero deaths (Velvet); Romania: ~1,100 killed, Ceaușescu executed. (c) Czechoslovakia: orderly transition to coalition government, free elections June 1990; Romania: NSF seized power, won May 1990 elections amid fraud allegations, former communists retained control. A wrong answer claiming both were "peaceful" or both led to "clean breaks" ignores the Romanian Securitate's role and the "stolen revolution" critique — a frequent board exam trap.

questions.q: Evaluate the argument: "The 1989 revolutions succeeded because Gorbachev deliberately engineered the collapse of the Eastern Bloc to save the Soviet Union." Support or refute with evidence.
questions.a: Refute. Evidence: (1) Gorbachev's 1988 UN speech announced non-intervention as principle, not strategy — he expected reformed socialist allies, not regime change. (2) He urged East German leader Honecker to reform (Oct 1989), not resign. (3) Soviet hardliners (Yazov, Kryuchkov) opposed the Sinatra Doctrine; Gorbachev faced coup risk (Aug 1991). (4) Economic burden: USSR subsidized Eastern Bloc via cheap oil/gas; collapse worsened Soviet economy. The revolutions were bottom-up; Gorbachev's contribution was negative (withholding coercion), not positive (engineering). A wrong answer accepting the "engineered collapse" thesis confuses structural permissive cause with intentional agency — a classic competitive-exam trap.

questions.q: Draft a 3-clause "Lesson from 1989" resolution for a Model UN committee on democratic transitions, drawing on the Eastern European experience. Each clause must reference a specific 1989 case.
questions.a: Sample resolution: (1) "Recognizing that negotiated round-table talks (Poland, Feb-Apr 1989) between incumbent regimes and opposition movements can produce legitimate power-sharing without violence, urges transitioning states to establish inclusive dialogue mechanisms before elections." (2) "Noting that the unilateral opening of borders (Hungary-Austria, Sept 1989) created irreversible momentum for change by enabling citizen exit and international scrutiny, calls on authoritarian states to respect freedom of movement as a catalyst for reform." (3) "Warning that revolutions hijacked by former security elites (Romania, Dec 1989) risk reproducing authoritarian structures, emphasizes the necessity of lustration and security-sector reform in post-transition constitutions." A poor answer offers generic platitudes ("support democracy") without anchoring clauses in specific 1989 mechanisms, showing inability to extract transferable political lessons.
